conditions.title: Cardiac Arrest
recognize: Unresponsive
Not breathing normally, or no breathing
No pulse
treat: Confirm scene safety and unresponsiveness
Begin CPR immediately — 30 compressions : 2 breaths, 100–120/min, full recoil
Attach the AED as soon as it arrives and follow its voice prompts
Continue CPR until the AED advises otherwise, rescuers are exhausted, or the patient is handed off to more advanced care
If the patient is hypothermic, extend pulse checks to 60 seconds and keep resuscitating — see Cold Exposure

conditions.title: Severe / Life-Threatening Bleeding
recognize: Spurting or steady heavy blood loss
Blood pooling faster than it can be absorbed
treat: Apply firm direct pressure with gauze; add more gauze on top if it soaks through, don't remove the first layer
If on a limb and direct pressure fails, apply a tourniquet 2–3 in above the wound (never on a joint); tighten until bleeding stops and note the time
Do not loosen a tourniquet once applied in the field
For deep wounds on the torso or junctional areas (groin/armpit) where a tourniquet can't be used, pack the wound with gauze and hold direct pressure

conditions.title: Anaphylaxis
recognize: Hives, swelling of face/lips/tongue, or widespread rash
Plus difficulty breathing, wheezing, throat tightness, or GI symptoms (vomiting, cramping)
Rapid onset after a sting, food, or medication
treat: Administer the epinephrine auto-injector into the outer thigh (can go through clothing); hold per the device's instructions
Position: lying flat with legs raised if dizzy/faint; sitting up if breathing is easier that way; recovery position if vomiting
May repeat a second dose after 5–15 minutes if there's no improvement and one is available
Antihistamine and inhaler are useful adjuncts but do not replace epinephrine
Evacuate even if symptoms fully resolve — a second wave (biphasic reaction) can follow hours later

conditions.title: Drowning / Near-Drowning
recognize: Submersion, panicked or silent struggling swimmer
Coughing, foam at the mouth, or altered mental status after a swim/flip
treat: Reach or throw before you go — don't become a second victim in the current
If not breathing, begin rescue breaths / CPR immediately, even before the patient is fully out of the water if it's safe to do so
Any submersion with coughing, altered mental status, or breathing trouble needs evaluation — delayed pulmonary edema can develop hours later even after an apparent full recovery

conditions.title: Suspected Spinal Injury
recognize: Significant mechanism — fall, high-speed flip, hard hit against rock or gear
Neck/back pain, numbness, tingling, weakness, or altered mental status
treat: Minimize movement; manually stabilize the head and neck in the position found
Do not move the patient unless there is immediate danger (fire, rising water, rockfall)
Assess and monitor circulation/sensation/motion in all four limbs

conditions.title: Long Bone Fracture (Closed)
recognize: Deformity, swelling, point tenderness
Inability to bear weight or use the limb
treat: Check circulation, sensation, and motion (CSM) distal to the injury before splinting
Splint in the position found using a SAM splint; immobilize the joints above and below the fracture
Recheck CSM after splinting
Ice and elevate if possible

conditions.title: Open / Compound Fracture
recognize: Bone visible, or a wound directly over a suspected fracture
treat: Control bleeding with direct pressure first
Do not push the bone back in
If evacuation will be delayed more than ~6 hours, gently irrigate the wound with clean water
Cover with a sterile dressing, then splint without putting pressure on the wound
Treat as high infection risk — this is the highest-priority fracture type

conditions.title: Joint Dislocation
recognize: Visible deformity at a joint, severe pain, loss of function
treat: Check CSM distal to the injury
Splint in the position found
Do not attempt to force it back into place unless a WFR-trained responder judges CSM is compromised and a specific reduction technique applies

conditions.title: Sprains & Strains
recognize: Pain, swelling, bruising around a joint
Some stability and weight-bearing usually still possible
treat: RICE — Rest, Ice (or cold river water), Compression wrap, Elevation
NSAID for pain/swelling per package directions
Reassess ability to bear weight before resuming activity; escalate if not improving in 24–48 hours

conditions.title: Minor Cuts & Scrapes
recognize: Shallow wound, controlled bleeding
treat: Irrigate thoroughly with clean water, remove debris
Antibiotic ointment, cover with a bandage
Change daily; watch for infection — increasing redness, warmth, pus, red streaking, fever

conditions.title: Deep Lacerations
recognize: Wound edges gape open, may extend into fat or muscle
treat: Control bleeding with direct pressure; irrigate thoroughly
If clean and under ~6–12 hours old, approximate the edges with wound-closure strips
Cover and monitor closely; evacuate if it can't be closed cleanly, crosses a joint, or shows infection signs

conditions.title: Blisters
recognize: Friction-related fluid pocket under the skin
treat: Clean the area; leave intact if possible
If painful or likely to tear, drain with a sterilized needle and leave the roof of skin in place
Cover with moleskin or a blister pad

conditions.title: Burns
recognize: Sun, stove/fire, or scald exposure
Redness, blistering, or (severe) white/charred/leathery skin
treat: Cool immediately with water for 10+ minutes; do not apply ice directly to the burn
Cover with a sterile non-stick dressing; do not pop blisters
NSAID for pain
Evacuate urgently if the burn is large, on the face/hands/genitals/joints, full-thickness, or wraps around a limb

conditions.title: Sunburn
recognize: Red, hot, tender skin; tight feeling; blistering and chills when severe
Reflected glare off the water burns the spots people forget — under the chin and nose, backs of the hands, ears, and lips
prevent: Broad-spectrum SPF 30+ reapplied every 2 hours and after every swim; don't skip ears, tops of feet, and the underside of the chin
Sun hoodie, wide-brim hat, UPF long sleeves, and sun gloves do more than lotion ever will — cover up
Zinc oxide on nose, lips, and ears; sunglasses to protect the eyes off the water glare
Take the midday break in shade when you can
treat: Cool the skin with water or cool wet compresses
Aloe or a plain moisturizer; rehydrate; NSAID for pain
Leave blisters intact; keep burned skin out of the sun and covered
conditions.note: Widespread blistering, fever, or a burn on a child — treat as a burn and monitor (see Wounds, Burns & Skin).

conditions.title: Chafing
recognize: Raw, stinging, reddened skin where skin or wet fabric rubs — inner thighs, groin, underarms, waistband, PFD edges, and bra lines
Salt, sand, and constant damp make it worse fast
prevent: Anti-chafe balm or petroleum jelly on friction zones before the day starts
Snug synthetic or wool base layers — no cotton; make sure the PFD and shorts actually fit
Rinse salt and grit off the skin and let seams dry
treat: Clean and dry the area
Barrier ointment (zinc oxide / diaper cream) or antibiotic ointment
Air it out at camp; pad the spot before the next day
conditions.note: If broken skin becomes redder, warm, or starts weeping pus, treat as an infection and watch it.

conditions.title: Heat Rash & Skin Rashes
recognize: Prickly rash or tiny bumps in sweaty, covered areas (heat rash / prickly heat)
Itchy red patches from plant contact or a new product (contact dermatitis)
prevent: Loose, breathable layers; keep skin as dry as conditions allow
Rinse sweat and sunscreen off at day's end
Don't brush bare skin against unfamiliar plants
treat: Cool, dry, and air out the area
Hydrocortisone cream for itch; antihistamine if it's widespread and itchy; calamine helps
Don't scratch — broken skin invites infection
conditions.note: A spreading rash with fever or blistering, or any facial/throat swelling with breathing trouble, is not a simple rash — see Life-Threatening Emergencies.

conditions.title: Dry & Cracked Hands
recognize: Tight, rough, splitting skin on knuckles, fingertips, and cuticles from sun, wind, sand, and endless wet-dry cycles
Deep cracks (fissures) at the fingertips that snag, sting, and bleed
prevent: Heavy hand balm morning and night and after every wash — this is the whole game
Gloves for rigging and rope work; go easy on harsh soap and hand sanitizer
A thick coat of balm under gloves or socks overnight lets hands recover
treat: Wash, dry, then seal with a thick occlusive balm (petroleum jelly / Aquaphor), heaviest at bedtime
For a deep painful crack, clean it and close it with liquid bandage / skin glue, or tape over ointment
Cover any split that could pick up dirt

conditions.title: Wet Feet & Immersion Foot
recognize: Pale, wrinkled, soft (macerated) skin from feet living in wet neoprene all day; tender, itchy, prone to cracking
Athlete's foot — itchy, peeling, cracked skin between the toes
Immersion (“trench”) foot in prolonged cases: numb, cold, blotchy feet that become painful and swollen on rewarming
prevent: Dry the feet out every chance — bare feet in camp, air and sun them at every stop
Keep one dry pair of socks and camp shoes/sandals reserved for evenings only
Foot or antifungal powder daily; rinse grit; rotate and dry booties and socks; keep toenails trimmed
treat: Get feet clean, dry, and warm; elevate them at camp
Antifungal cream or powder for athlete's foot; barrier cream on macerated skin
Treat cracks and blisters as wounds — clean, protect, watch for infection
conditions.note: Immersion foot with persistent numbness, swelling, or spreading redness/pus needs to be monitored closely and evacuated if it worsens.

conditions.title: Chapped Lips
recognize: Dry, cracked, peeling, sometimes bleeding lips from sun and wind
prevent: SPF lip balm, reapplied often; hat brim for shade; stay hydrated
treat: Occlusive lip balm; stop licking the lips (it makes it worse); let cracks heal under balm

conditions.title: Concussion / Head Injury
recognize: Mechanism to the head, plus any of: confusion, headache, dizziness, nausea, memory gaps, any loss of consciousness (even brief)
treat: Rest; recheck neuro status frequently over the next 24 hours — this is the key task
Use acetaminophen rather than NSAIDs for pain (avoids masking a bleed)
Avoid re-injury
conditions.note: Evacuate immediately for any: loss of consciousness, worsening confusion, unequal pupils, repeated vomiting, or seizure.

conditions.title: Hypothermia — Mild
recognize: Shivering, alert, mild confusion, cold to the touch
treat: Remove wet clothing, insulate with dry layers and a sleeping bag
Warm sweet drinks if fully alert
Light activity to generate heat; shelter from wind

conditions.title: Hypothermia — Moderate / Severe
recognize: Shivering stops
Confusion, lethargy, slurred speech, loss of coordination
Severe: unresponsive, weak or absent pulse
treat: Handle gently — rough movement can trigger a fatal arrhythmia
Remove wet clothing (cut it off rather than moving the limbs if needed)
Insulate fully, including the head; active rewarming with warm packs at the neck, armpits, and groin
Do not give food or fluids unless fully alert; do not massage the extremities
If no pulse is found after a full 60-second check, begin CPR and continue — hypothermic patients can survive prolonged arrest: not dead until warm and dead

conditions.title: Frostnip / Frostbite
recognize: Numbness, white or waxy skin
Frostbite: tissue is hard/wooden — actually frozen
treat: Frostnip: rewarm with body heat
Frostbite: do NOT rewarm if there's any chance of refreezing — refreezing causes far worse damage than staying frozen
If refreezing can be prevented, rewarm only in a stable warm water bath; expect severe pain on rewarming and protect the area afterward

conditions.title: Heat Exhaustion
recognize: Heavy sweating, weakness, nausea, headache, dizziness
Mental status close to normal
treat: Move to shade, remove excess clothing
Cool with water and fanning
Rehydrate with water plus electrolytes; rest
Evacuate if not improving within 30–60 minutes

conditions.title: Heat Stroke
recognize: Altered mental status — confusion, combativeness, or unconsciousness — combined with feeling hot
May or may not still be sweating
treat: Aggressive cooling is the priority — immerse in river water if it can be done safely, or wet the skin and fan
Ice packs at the neck, armpits, and groin
Treat as a true emergency

conditions.title: Dehydration
recognize: Thirst, dark urine, fatigue, headache, dizziness
treat: Oral rehydration with water plus electrolytes
Monitor urine color and output

conditions.title: Gastrointestinal Illness
recognize: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, cramping, possibly fever
treat: Aggressive oral rehydration with water plus electrolytes; rest; bland food as tolerated
An anti-diarrheal can be used for symptom control if there's no high fever or blood in the stool
Strict hand hygiene and separate personal eating/drinking gear — this spreads fast through a shared kitchen
Evacuate if fluids can't be kept down for 24+ hours, dehydration is severe, or there's high fever or blood in stool/vomit

conditions.title: Hangover
recognize: Headache, nausea, fatigue, dehydration after alcohol use
treat: Rehydrate with water plus electrolytes
Acetaminophen or NSAID for headache (not both), bland food, rest, time
If symptoms are severe or don't fit the usual pattern, reconsider heat illness, dehydration, or GI illness instead

conditions.title: Rattlesnake Bite
recognize: Puncture marks, immediate pain, swelling that spreads over time
treat: Keep the patient calm and still; immobilize the bitten limb below heart level
Remove jewelry and tight clothing before swelling progresses
Mark and time the leading edge of swelling on the skin if possible
Do NOT cut the wound, suck out venom, apply a tourniquet, or apply ice — all worsen outcomes and are outdated advice

conditions.title: Scorpion Sting
recognize: Sharp localized pain and swelling
Bark scorpion stings can cause systemic symptoms — numbness beyond the site, trouble breathing — especially in children
treat: Clean the site, cold pack, pain control
Monitor closely for systemic symptoms; evacuate urgently if they appear

conditions.title: Insect Sting (Bee / Wasp)
recognize: Localized pain, swelling, redness at the sting site
treat: Scrape out a stinger if present (don't pinch it — that injects more venom)
Cold pack, antihistamine, NSAID for pain
Watch for signs of anaphylaxis — see Life-Threatening Emergencies

signals: Move to that side — never point at the hazard
rescue: Tell the swimmer where to go.
Paddle, oar, branch, hand — from a stance you won't be pulled out of.
Bag past and across the swimmer. Rope over the shoulder, never wrapped.
Bring a boat. Stern or line, not the oar blade.
swim: Never stand in current above the knee.
Swim at it hard, head up, get on top of it.
Downstream corners; if held, ball up and take the deep outflow.
Do your self-rescue in the first minute. Hands stop working after ten.
